title: Microsoft Foundry, from provisioning to model deployment
summary: This intermediate-level module teaches you to plan and provision a Microsoft Foundry project, select a suitable model, create a deployment, validate its behavior, and prepare it for application use. After completing it, you can follow a controlled path from an approved cloud scope to a tested model endpoint.
objectives: Explain the roles of a Foundry resource, a project, a model, and a deployment.
Perform a preflight review of access, region, capacity, governance, and model requirements before provisioning.
Provision a project within an approved organizational and billing scope.
Evaluate an available model against task, licensing, interface, and capacity requirements.
Create and validate a model deployment without exposing its credentials.
Record the information an application team needs to consume, monitor, replace, or retire a deployment.

sections.title: Level and assumed knowledge
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you understand basic cloud concepts such as regions, access permissions, billing scopes, resource containers, network requests, and model inference. It does not assume that you have previously provisioned Microsoft Foundry or deployed a model there.

The outcome is practical. Before this module, you might recognize Foundry as a place to work with models. After it, you can plan the required boundaries, provision a project, select an appropriate model, deploy it, validate the resulting endpoint, and prepare an operational handoff.

sections.title: Understand the resource chain
paragraphs: Keep four concepts separate. A Foundry resource supplies the cloud context and governance boundary used by Foundry. A project is the workspace in which a team organizes its model work. A model is the selected inference capability. A deployment is a configured, callable instance of that model.

Provisioning and deployment are therefore different operations. Provisioning establishes the resource and project in an approved location and administrative scope. Deployment selects a model and makes it available for inference under a deployment-specific endpoint or connection.

This distinction helps with troubleshooting. If a project cannot be created, investigate scope, region, permissions, and policy. If the project exists but a model cannot be deployed, investigate model availability, capacity, deployment eligibility, and the selected region.
sections.callout: Do not treat project creation as proof that every model can be deployed there. Model availability and capacity must be checked separately.

sections.title: Perform a provisioning preflight
paragraphs: Start with the intended workload rather than the interface. Record the task the model must perform, the expected input and output forms, who may use it, the sensitivity of its data, and how success will be tested. These requirements provide a basis for choosing a model and rejecting unsuitable options.

Confirm the approved billing scope, resource container, region, and access permissions before creating anything. Also identify the person or team authorized to approve cost, model terms, data handling, and production use. If any of those decisions is unresolved, pause rather than creating an unowned resource.

Check that the intended model is offered for the selected region and deployment context. Review the model information presented by Foundry, including intended uses, limitations, applicable terms, supported interfaces, and any capacity requirement. Availability in a model list does not by itself establish suitability for the workload.

Define a simple acceptance test before deployment. Include representative inputs, expected output characteristics, prohibited behavior, and a failure condition. A deployment is technically reachable when it accepts a request, but it is acceptable for use only when it also meets the workload's stated criteria.

sections.title: Provision the Foundry project
paragraphs: Use the documented project-creation flow to select or create the Foundry resource that will back the project, then create the project within the approved scope. Choose only the region and organizational placement approved during the preflight. Use locally defined naming and tagging conventions if your organization has them.

After creation, verify the project boundary before adding a deployment. Confirm that you are in the intended project, that its backing resource and region match the approved plan, and that the expected collaborators have only the access required for their roles.

Record the project owner, purpose, region, billing owner, intended data classification, and review date in the team's operational record. This record is separate from the technical resource. It allows another person to determine why the project exists and who can authorize changes or retirement.

Do not continue if the project appears in an unexpected scope or region. Creating a model deployment in the wrong project compounds the error and can expose the workload to an unapproved policy, access, or cost boundary.

sections.title: Select a model for the workload
paragraphs: Inspect the models available to the project and compare them with the written workload requirements. Begin with task fit and supported input and output forms. Then review limitations, applicable terms, regional availability, capacity, and the deployment choices Foundry presents for that model.

Prefer an explicit decision record over a vague statement that one model seemed best. Record the chosen model, the alternatives considered, the acceptance criteria, known limitations, and the reason for selection. This makes a later model replacement reviewable.

Do not infer that two models are interchangeable because they accept similar prompts. Their output behavior, limitations, terms, capacity needs, and interfaces can differ. Test the exact model and deployment that the application will call.

sections.title: Create the model deployment
paragraphs: Open the selected model's deployment flow and choose only an option that Foundry makes available for the current project and region. Review the displayed model, region, capacity implications, and applicable terms before confirming. If required capacity is unavailable, return to planning rather than silently changing the workload requirement.

Give the deployment an identity that follows the organization's naming convention and distinguishes its purpose or environment. Avoid placing secrets, personal data, or sensitive business information in the deployment identity or descriptive metadata.

Submit the deployment and wait for its reported state to indicate that it is ready before testing it. A submitted operation is not the same as a usable deployment. If creation fails, preserve the reported error and recheck permissions, availability, capacity, region, and policy rather than repeatedly submitting the same request.

Once ready, identify the connection information the approved application needs. Treat credentials as secrets. Do not paste them into source code, shared documents, test prompts, or operational notes. Provide them through the organization's approved secret-handling process.

sections.title: Validate and hand off the deployment
paragraphs: First perform a connectivity check with a non-sensitive input. Confirm that the request reaches the intended deployment and produces a response. This proves basic reachability, not model quality or production readiness.

Next run the acceptance test defined during the preflight. Use representative inputs and compare the outputs with the recorded criteria. Test relevant failure cases, such as malformed or unsupported input, without using confidential data unless the workload and its data handling have been approved for that purpose.

Record the tested deployment identity, model, project, region, test date, acceptance result, known limitations, owner, and retirement or review trigger. Give the application team only the endpoint details and access path it needs. Do not include secret values in the handoff record.

Prepare a replacement and recovery plan before production use. Keep the previous acceptable deployment available when organizational policy and cost constraints permit, verify a replacement before directing application traffic to it, and define who can approve the switch. If validation fails, do not promote the new deployment.

After traffic moves or an experiment ends, review unused deployments and resources for retirement. Confirm dependencies and retention obligations before deletion. Record the decision so that an apparently unused deployment is not removed without an accountable review.
sections.callout: A successful response proves connectivity. Production readiness also requires documented quality, security, governance, ownership, and recovery checks.

sections.title: Apply the end-to-end sequence
paragraphs: The complete sequence is to define the workload, confirm governance and regional constraints, define acceptance tests, provision the correct resource and project, verify their boundaries, evaluate available models, create the selected deployment, wait for readiness, test connectivity, run acceptance tests, secure connection information, document ownership, and prepare replacement and retirement procedures.

Each stage has a distinct completion condition. Provisioning is complete when the intended project exists in the approved boundary and ownership is recorded. Deployment is complete when the selected model has a ready deployment. Validation is complete only when the exact deployment passes the predetermined tests. Handoff is complete when an application team can connect through an approved access path and operators know how to review, replace, or retire the deployment.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes provisioning from model deployment?
choices: Provisioning establishes the resource and project boundary, while deployment creates a callable instance of a selected model.
Provisioning tests model output quality, while deployment assigns project permissions.
Provisioning and deployment are two names for the same operation.
Provisioning begins only after an application has entered production.
questions.explanation: The module defines provisioning as establishing the Foundry resource and project context. Deployment selects and configures a model so that it can be called for inference.

questions.prompt: What should happen before resources are created?
choices: The team should select whichever model appears first.
The team should confirm workload requirements, scope, region, permissions, governance ownership, and acceptance criteria.
The team should distribute credentials to all collaborators.
The team should assume that every listed model is available in every project.
questions.explanation: The preflight establishes the workload, approved boundary, access, ownership, model constraints, and tests before provisioning begins.

questions.prompt: A new deployment returns a response to a test request. What has this established?
choices: The deployment is ready for every production workload.
The model has no limitations.
Basic connectivity works, but quality and production-readiness checks are still required.
The deployment can safely process every data classification.
questions.explanation: A successful request proves basic reachability. The module requires separate acceptance, governance, security, ownership, and recovery checks.

questions.prompt: How should deployment credentials be handled during handoff?
choices: Place them directly in application source code.
Include them in the shared operational record.
Send them as part of a test prompt.
Provide them through the organization's approved secret-handling process.
questions.explanation: The module says to treat credentials as secrets and to keep secret values out of source code, shared documents, prompts, and operational notes.

questions.prompt: What is the correct response when a replacement deployment fails its acceptance test?
choices: Promote it because it is technically reachable.
Do not promote it, preserve the evidence, and investigate the failed criteria.
Delete every previous deployment immediately.
Change the acceptance criteria after seeing the output.
questions.explanation: The module states that a new deployment must pass predetermined acceptance tests before promotion. A failure should be investigated rather than hidden by changing the criteria.
